newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak cen. bank reaffirms tight policy - paper.
newsitem.headline: Slovak cen. bank reaffirms tight policy - paper.

text.p: A senior Slovak central bank (NBS) official has reaffirmed the bank's committment to strict monetary policy and maintaining a stable currency, leading economic daily Hospodarske Noviny reported on Tuesday.

"The aim is to create a base for maintaining the main goals of the monetary policy -- a stable currency and stable foreign exchange rate within the set fluctuation band," Elena Kohutikova, head of the NBS's monetary department told the paper in an interview.
"The NBS's measures are naturally unpopular, but we consider them necessary for moderating the dynamics of the current account deficit caused by consumption-led growth last year," she said.

Kohutikova said preliminary results showed that some unfavourable tendencies, such as rapid money supply growth and credit expansion, had stopped or moderated significantly last year due to the tough policy.
She added that the current plus/minus 7.0 percent fluctuation band within which the NBS fixes the crown daily against its mark/dollar basket should be sufficient.
Some banks and businesses, and even government officials, have complained about the NBS's tough stance but Kohutikova said it was too early to consider a change.
"Despite favourable developments continuing this year, one month is too short a time to draw any relevant conclusions about a further development," she said.
Kohutikova also reitereated a call for banks in Slovakia to adjust to the NBS policy.

"I presume the banks will improve coordination between their individual divisions and pay more attention to securing their liquidity to adjust to the central bank's stricter monetary policy," Kohutikova said.

She added that a cautious credit policy by banks should be gradually reflected in Slovakia's trade balance and current account. A further consumption-led credit expansion would further stretch Slovakia's increasing internal and external indebtedness, she said.

"If the government's goals are to be fulfilled along with (sustaining) the stable currency, the credit market will have to step back, and other ways of raising needed capital should be sought," Kohutikova said.

She said the NBS presumed that many firms would seek strategic partners to get needed capital and new technologies, which may lead to a boost in direct capital inflow. This, in the NBS's view, would be the safest source to cover the current account gap.
"The central bank alone cannot solve all these problems, it is not omnipotent," Kohutikova said.
